item.title: AI-based digital pathology defines spatial border ecosystems in triple-negative breast cancer
item.dc:creator: Hang Zhang
Fan Yang
Pu Tian
Han Wang
Ying Xu
Xiao-Hui Zhu
Xue-Pei Li

item.description:
Authors: Hang Zhang, Fan Yang, Pu Tian, Han Wang, Ying Xu, Xiao-Hui Zhu, Xue-Pei Li, Shen Zhao, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaei6252
Abstract: The invasive tumor border in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is currently poorly understood. We integrated digital pathology and spatial multi-omics to define border ecosystems in TNBC. AI-based digital pathology identified five border ecosystems, three associated with prognosis. Spatial multi-omics analyses further resolved the spatial niche, molecular mechanisms and clinical relevance of these ecosystems. Immune-infiltrated borders contain a triadic immune niche associated with favorable prognosis and immunotherapy sensitivity. Tumor–stroma borders harbor a MIF + fibroblast exclusion niche that blocks immune infiltration and suppresses T cells function, predicting poor prognosis. Tumor–adipose borders, featured an FLT1 + endothelial niche, promote hypoxia, vascular leakage, and tumor dissemination. Targeting this niche inhibits tumor progression. Collectively, these findings establish a spatial resource that might enable border-directed therapeutic strategies in TNBC.

item.title: An engineered cohesion system reduces errors in aged mammalian eggs
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Webster
Halima Yusuf
Nina Schweizer
Chloe Charalambous
Eike Urs Mönnich
Heike Eckel
Rüdiger Moltrecht

item.description:
Authors: Alexandre Webster, Halima Yusuf, Nina Schweizer, Chloe Charalambous, Eike Urs Mönnich, Heike Eckel, Rüdiger Moltrecht, Martyn Blayney, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 982-989
Abstract: In humans, female fertility declines rapidly from approximately 35 years onward owing to a steep increase in eggs in which chromosomes have split prematurely or that harbor an incorrect number of chromosomes (aneuploid eggs). A leading cause of age-related aneuploidy in eggs is the premature separation of sister chromatids (PSSC), which is caused by a loss of cohesin from chromosomes. In this study, we created an artificial cohesion system that reduces PSSC in aged mouse eggs. We further engineered a separase-cleavable sequence into the system, allowing for its scheduled deactivation during anaphase. We demonstrated that the artificial cohesion system could be adapted to tether human chromosomes, providing a proof of principle for the future development of approaches to reduce PSSC in eggs from women of advanced reproductive age.

item.description:
Authors: Trenton Dailey-Chwalibóg, Andrew Mertens, Kelsey Fehr, Chi-Hung Shu, April Jauhal, Melissa B. Manus, Lishi Deng, Laeticia Celine Toe, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Article number: eaee9284
Abstract: Human milk (HM) composition is variable to support changing infant needs and is influenced by maternal diet and health. We harmonized HM data from three randomized trials in Burkina Faso (MISAME-III), Pakistan (Mumta-LW), and Tanzania (ELICIT) within the International Milk Composition (IMiC) Consortium to test how maternal nutrition affects HM composition. Balanced energy-protein (BEP) supplements or nicotinamide given to lactating mothers increased milk B vitamins, whereas macronutrients, oligosaccharides, bioactive proteins, and microbiome composition were physiologically buffered. Metabolomic and proteomic analyses revealed shifts in vitamin-related metabolites, triglyceride profiles, and intracellular protein representation. In a MISAME-III subset, maternal and infant blood showed concordant changes. Postnatal BEP improved infant growth only in the more undernourished cohort. Improved milk micronutrient quality across settings supports extending maternal supplementation into lactation.

item.description:
Authors: Manisha Caleb, Themiya Nanayakkara, Benjamin W. Stappers, Inés Pastor-Marazuela, Ilya S. Khrykin, Karl Glazebrook, Nicolas Tejos, J. Xavier Prochaska, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 990-995
Abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients from extragalactic sources. Their frequency and polarization properties are affected by plasma and magnetic fields along the line of sight to Earth. We report radio observations of FRB 20240304B and near-infrared follow-up to identify its host galaxy. The host is a low-mass, clumpy, star-forming galaxy at redshift 2.148 ± 0.0013, corresponding to 3 billion years after the Big Bang. This FRB occurred during the peak of cosmic star formation and probes ionized gas over ~80% of cosmic history. The highly scattered burst emission implies that there is a population of FRBs that are undetected by current surveys.

item.title: Mechanisms of nucleosome disruption shape epigenetic inheritance pathway choice
item.dc:creator: Oliver Willhoft
Milos A. Cvetkovic

item.description:
Authors: Oliver Willhoft, Milos A. Cvetkovic, Fernando R. Rosas Bringas, Dolores Jurado-Santiago, Robert Ciaran Mackenzie Frater, Kimberly Quililan, Thomas Pühringer, Daniel Ramirez Montero, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaek0813
Abstract: Maintaining cell identity requires duplicating the genome and epigenome during S phase. As DNA is copied, histones extracted from parental nucleosomes are transferred to nascent strands, which preserves the position of epigenetic marks. How the replisome coordinates these processes is unclear. Using reconstitution with purified yeast proteins, kinetic measurements, structural biology, mass spectrometry and genomics, we examined nucleosome-replisome encounter and histone transfer. Parental nucleosomes can be unwrapped ahead of the fork by the MCM helicase, aided by FACT and Ctf4, or by Tof1. Nucleosomal DNA unwrapping by MCM creates a FACT binding site, helping strip histones off DNA. Ctf4 enhances FACT-stimulated histone extraction, retains parental histones and hands them to Tof1, en route to lagging-strand redeposition. Thus, extraction via Ctf4 commits histones to lagging-strand transfer.

item.dc:creator: Haipeng Luo
Fengzhou Tan

Matías Carvajal
item.description:
Authors: Haipeng Luo, Fengzhou Tan, Zhangfeng Ma, Kejie Chen, Jian Zhang, Xin Wang, Shiqing Xu, Matías Carvajal, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 1002-1006
Abstract: Rough fault segments typically terminate giant earthquakes but are rarely reported to foster them. However, rupture characteristics of the 2025 moment magnitude ( M w ) 8.8 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake are consistent with initiation in a rough zone. Its early rupture was sluggish, lasting ~50 seconds with limited slip but strong, scattered high-frequency radiation. Rupture then propagated southward into a smoother segment, producing >20 meters slip with less intense high-frequency radiation. Using also the rupture characteristics of four M w 7+ foreshocks and aftershocks, we reveal variably sized seismic patches within the rough zone. We interpret these behaviors as manifestations of stress or frictional heterogeneities on the rough segment that favor localized failures yet can foster a giant rupture when spatially connected to a smooth, locked neighboring segment, a scenario previously underrecognized and meriting consideration in seismic hazard assessments.

item.title: Integrating established and emerging tools to assess wildlife condition from the ground, up
item.dc:creator: Michelle R. Shero
David W. Johnston
Amy L. Kirkham
Jennifer M. Burns

item.description:
Authors: Michelle R. Shero, David W. Johnston, Amy L. Kirkham, Jennifer M. Burns, Caroline L. Rzucidlo, Daniel P. Costa, K.C. Bierlich
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 950-959
Abstract: Metabolic energy links individual physiology to population-level dynamics, making wildlife body condition a cornerstone of conservation science. Emerging technologies, including unoccupied aircraft systems, make remote assessment of animal condition possible at unprecedented scales, and physiologically grounded validation is essential for strong inference. Here we examine the strengths and challenges of traditional and remote methods, using a comparative perspective that emphasizes both lipid and lean mass dynamics in evaluating wildlife health. We provide a framework that integrates complementary approaches to assess wildlife condition across diverse systems, matching emerging methods with the required physiological resolution, species characteristics, and temporal and spatial scales, while enhancing research ethics. Expanding capacity to track wildlife energetics from individuals to populations requires novel approaches and is vital for conservation in a changing world.

item.description:
Authors: Yujie Ren, Xiao-Xu Zhu, Yaxin Wang, An Wang, Bowen Zhang, Jing Lou, Cheng Zhu, Dawei Jiang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Article number: eadx9551
Abstract: Argonaute-2 (AGO2)–mediated RNA silencing contributes to antiviral defenses in plants and insects and may contribute to mammalian immunity, too. However, it is unknown whether AGO2 is modified upon infection or inflammation in mammals. We identified that the ubiquitin ligase RING-finger protein 126 (RNF126) interacts with and ubiquitinates AGO2 to enhance its small interfering RNA or microRNA loading. Using data from cells in vitro and mouse tissues, we propose that RNF126 is induced by type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling and promotes the ability of AGO2 to silence proinflammatory genes and inhibit viral replication. Lipid nanoparticle delivery of RNF126 mRNA to mice inhibited inflammation and viral replication. These findings identify cross-talk of IFN-based immune signaling and AGO2-mediated RNA silencing and suggest that the RNF126-AGO2 axis helps to balance inflammatory and antiviral immune protection.

item.title: Counter-ion confinement reverses ion selectivity in subnanometer channels
item.dc:creator: Fangmeng Sheng
Liang Ge
Bin Wu
Xingya Li
Tongwen Xu
item.description:
Authors: Fangmeng Sheng, Liang Ge, Bin Wu, Xingya Li, Tongwen Xu
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 1013-1019
Abstract: Ion transport in nano- and subnanometer channels is central to processes such as ion separation, energy conversion and storage, and nanofluidics. Conventionally, positively charged nanochannels favor anion transport and vice versa. We report that cationic covalent organic framework membranes with sub–one-nanometer channels exhibit selective cation transport. This reversal in selectivity arises from a counter-ion confinement effect, which inverts the electrostatic environment inside the channel wall and creates a secondary confinement region. The counter-ion confinement mechanism concomitantly suppresses coexisting ion competition in mixed-salt systems, enabling membranes to retain high selectivity under practical separation conditions. Our findings provide a design strategy for creating adaptive and highly selective membranes for precise ion transport and separation.

item.title: A tryptophan cation radical determines radical transfer kinetics and catalytic rate in a ribonucleotide reductase
item.dc:creator: Nejc Nagelj
Chang Cui
Kenichi Yokoyama
JoAnne Stubbe
Daniel G. Nocera
item.description:
Authors: Nejc Nagelj, Chang Cui, Kenichi Yokoyama, JoAnne Stubbe, Daniel G. Nocera
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 967-971
Abstract: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) is the sole enzyme responsible for de novo deoxynucleotide synthesis for DNA replication and repair. In the Escherichia coli class Ia RNR, a radical must traverse 32 angstroms along a pathway composed of amino acids spanning β and α subunits to complete each turnover. By incorporating unnatural amino acids to alter reduction potentials of pathway tyrosine residues, we (i) perturb the rates of radical transfer and show that they match the rates of deoxynucleotide production and (ii) directly observe a tryptophan cation radical (W 48 + •) as a kinetically competent pathway intermediate. Together, these results establish that radical transfer through W 48 in α 2 β 2 is the rate-limiting process, which controls the enzymatic activity of E. coli RNR.

Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Article number: eaeh2982
Abstract: The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. We describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which uses free-atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges, from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active-site architecture that incorporates a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases, we obtained active catalysts in zero-shot 96 construct design campaigns.

item.dc:creator: Mathieu Desaunay

item.description:
Authors: Mathieu Desaunay, Tara L. Peters, Evangelia Matenoglou, Beau Baars, Bijaya Gaire, Ana Orive-Ramos, Li Ren, Joseph P. Lyssikatos, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaed6493
Abstract: Targeting the RAS/MAPK pathway has long been constrained by dose-limiting toxicity in normal tissues at doses required for durable tumor control. Although Type 1.5 RAF inhibitors improved selectivity in BRAF(V600X)-monomer tumors, a comparable strategy for RAF dimer-driven cancers, including those with RAS mutations, has been lacking. We describe ELV-3111, a potent Type 1 RAF inhibitor that inhibits RAF dimers and exploits binding kinetics for tumor selectivity. ELV-3111 primes RAF in normal tissues, and its rapid dissociation during drug clearance generates drug-free RAF dimers that paradoxically activate MAPK signaling. RAS-mutant tumors are spared, where RAF is already primed. Combined with a MEK inhibitor, ELV-3111 restored normal tissue signaling while deepening tumor pathway inhibition, producing regressions across RAS- and BRAF-mutant experimental models. Thus, inhibitor dissociation kinetics provide a generalizable source of therapeutic index.

Abstract: Much has been written about how the social contract between science and society in the United States is in crisis. According to its terms, research will yield broad economic, health, and security benefits to the very public that funds it. But this relationship depends on public trust in science, its systems, and the scientists themselves, and therein lies the problem. Beyond making discoveries and publishing results, scientists shape their own culture, and that is where some changes may be the key to rebuilding public trust.

Authors: April Jauhal, Bianca Cordazzo-Vargas, Daniel Sunko, Pratima Niroula, Lishi Deng, Laeticia Celine Toe, Ameer Muhammad, Aneela Pasha, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Article number: eaee7240
Abstract: The mammary gland produces nutrient-rich human milk (HM), yet how mammary functional state shapes HM composition and infant outcomes remains poorly understood. We used HM multiomics, including metabolomics, proteomics, micronutrients, macronutrients, and HM oligosaccharides, across 1543 samples from three cohorts, including two randomized trials, as a noninvasive readout of mammary functional state. Trajectory modeling and multiomic integration showed that maternal supplementation improved recovery from early growth faltering and revealed a shared HM compositional axis linking maternal nutrition to infant growth. Machine learning, with Human Protein Atlas–informed proteomics, identified seven HM biomarkers reflecting variation across key mammary domains, indexing milk synthesis, barrier integrity, and immune-repair activity. Elevated valerylcarnitine and low pantothenic acid emerged as metabolic signals linking mammary functional state to infant growth.

Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 1020-1026
Abstract: Despite the importance of divergent synthesis to obtain different isomers for medicinal and material chemistry, divergent stereocontrol over four distinct selectivity factors remains a fundamental challenge. The telomerization reaction is limited to the transformation of simple unfunctionalized 1,3-dienes to circumvent intractable stereoisomeric mixtures. Here, we report an orthogonal telomerization platform using linear functionalized 1,3-dienes as the substrates, which simultaneously dictates geometric, regio-, diastereo-, and enantioselectivities. We prepared diverse types of γ-amino esters from identical, readily available unsaturated esters and amines via synergistic palladium and acid catalysis, with each precisely obtained out of hundreds of potential telomers. We developed several chiral phosphoramidite ligands to promote the transformation. This study showcases the potential of multidimensional stereomanipulation for the industrially valuable telomerization reaction.

item.dc:creator: Sangwoo Han
YoungHee Kim
Jaewoo Kim
Avinash Nayak

Jonathan Ajo-Franklin
item.description:
Authors: Sangwoo Han, YoungHee Kim, Jaewoo Kim, Avinash Nayak, Fu Yin, Jonathan Ajo-Franklin
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 996-1001
Abstract: Small earthquakes [i.e., those of magnitude ( M ) <3] are commonly modeled as simple circular ruptures, leaving the fine-scale spatial attributes of rupture dynamics unresolved. We used near-source distributed acoustic sensing to image the millisecond-scale rupture of an M 2 earthquake within a swarm sequence in California’s Brawley Seismic Zone. Inverting fiber-derived apparent source time functions revealed two distinct rupture episodes separated by 42 milliseconds, reflecting rupture arrest followed by dynamic renucleation. Analysis of a 3-hour sequence showed adjacent, largely nonoverlapping fault patches activated in succession, forming complementary slip partitioning. These fragmented failure patterns within the M 2 rupture and its sequence limited rupture growth, consistent with the absence of a dominant mainshock. Microearthquakes, which are now accessible by fiber-optic sensing, provide direct constraints on fault mechanics across scales bridging laboratory experiments and large earthquakes.

Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 1007-1012
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal’s assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing’s most important challenges.

item.description:
Authors: Yongqiang Zhang, Xian Wang, Jun Xia, Congcong Li, Xiaojie Li, Zhenwu Xu, Jing Tian, Gang Zhao, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6827; Pages: 1027-1032
Abstract: Global warming is expected to accelerate the hydrological cycle, yet its impact on terrestrial water availability is uncertain. Using assimilated streamflow observations from 150 major basins and satellite data for over 1.2 million water bodies, we show a global-scale synchronized decline of streamflow and surface water storage during the 2023–2024 record-warm period, the largest reduction since 1991. South America accounted for 70.4 ± 4.2% of the global streamflow decline. This abrupt depletion was driven by compound ocean–atmosphere forcing, in which concurrent El Niño and tropical North Atlantic warming triggered large-scale atmospheric subsidence, moisture divergence, and amplified drought. These findings reveal that extreme warming can induce abrupt water losses even in humid regions, underscoring a critical vulnerability of global hydrology and water security.

Yumin Li
Guitao Shi
Liuqian Yu
Yujue Wang
Senchao Lai
Yang Zhou
Yingyi Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Xu Yu, Yumin Li, Guitao Shi, Liuqian Yu, Yujue Wang, Senchao Lai, Yang Zhou, Yingyi Zhang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 901-906
Abstract: Atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is a critical nutrient source for marine ecosystems, but its organic nitrogen (ON) component remains poorly quantified. We measured ON in marine aerosols collected during 21 research cruises transecting multiple ocean basins and both hemispheric high latitudes. We used these observations to constrain and evaluate an atmospheric chemistry model with updated ON sources and sinks, enabling global mapping of ON deposition. The model estimated annual ON deposition to oceans at 12.8 (4.0 to 22.7) teragrams of nitrogen per year (Tg N year −1 ), contributing 27% (11 to 40%) of total N deposition. Marine emissions supply 3.9 (0.7 to 6.9) Tg N year −1 (30%) of deposited ON, while terrestrial sources contribute 8.9 (3.3 to 15.7) Tg N year −1 (70%). In N-limited regions such as the central Atlantic and Indonesian seas, ON accounts for ~50% of total N deposition.

item.title: Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality
item.dc:creator: S. Kumar
E. Rosenberg
A. Grajales Dau
R. G. Cortiñas

A. Zalcman
item.description:
Authors: S. Kumar, E. Rosenberg, A. Grajales Dau, R. G. Cortiñas, D. Maslov, R. Oliver, A. Zalcman, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 870-874
Abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. To examine many-body contextuality, we implement the N -player Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger game and separately solve a two-dimensional hidden linear function problem, advancing the state of the art on fidelity and system size in both tasks. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.

item.title: Divergent activation of the RXFP1 relaxin receptor by protein and small-molecule agonists
item.dc:creator: James Osei-Owusu
Tristan Girbau
Xunan Wang
Jeffrey S. Smith
Pengxiang Shen

item.description:
Authors: James Osei-Owusu, Tristan Girbau, Xunan Wang, Jeffrey S. Smith, Pengxiang Shen, Sarah C. Erlandson, Amanda K. Williamson, Xiaojing Cong, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Article number: eaei0135
Abstract: The relaxin receptor RXFP1 is a therapeutic target owing to its potential benefits in the treatment of fibrosis and heart failure. Protein and small-molecule agonists are currently in midstage clinical trials for various forms of heart disease. In this work, we present three cryo–electron microscopy structures of RXFP1: ligand-free, bound to the native agonist relaxin-2, and bound to the small-molecule drug candidate AZD5462. These structures reveal that relaxin-2 engages the receptor’s ectodomain, whereas AZD5462 binds to the transmembrane domain. Together with hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we show that relaxin-2 induces reorganization of the linker domain into a helical secondary structure. By contrast, AZD5462 stabilizes an active conformation through a distinct set of conformational rearrangements. Altogether, our findings define divergent activation mechanisms for protein and small-molecule agonists of RXFP1.

item.title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
item.dc:creator: Dylan G. E. Gomes
Lisa G. Crozier
James J. Ruzicka
David D. Huff
Joshua D. Stewart
item.description:
Authors: Dylan G. E. Gomes, Lisa G. Crozier, James J. Ruzicka, David D. Huff, Joshua D. Stewart
Journal: Science; Article number: eaeb1122
Abstract: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.

item.title: Angular momentum transfer from an optical vortex to an atomic rotor
item.dc:creator: Yu-Lung Tang
Ryan Tollefsen
Neha Yadav
Michael W. Zuerch
Hartmut Häffner
item.description:
Authors: Yu-Lung Tang, Ryan Tollefsen, Neha Yadav, Michael W. Zuerch, Hartmut Häffner
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 890-894
Abstract: Light carries angular momentum in two forms: spin, associated with polarization, and orbital, associated with helical wavefronts. Whereas spin angular momentum underlies well-known atomic selection rules, the role of orbital angular momentum (OAM) in light-matter interaction continues to be discussed in the literature. In this work, we investigate OAM transfer from a vortex laser beam to a trapped-ion quantum rotor using rotational sidebands of the electric quadrupole transition of 40 Ca + . We directly observe coherent transfer of optical OAM into quantized rotation and identify distinct selection rules for different rotational sidebands. This observation provides experimental evidence for a scale-dependent separation of angular momentum transfer pathways in light-matter interactions. Further, our work elucidates the previously reported modified selection rules in trapped-ion experiments, establishing a unified framework for twisted light–matter interactions.

item.title: Quiet within, chaos without: Turbulence shelters drive selective particle capture and release
item.dc:creator: Matteo Sabato
Sarah Chong
Yaocheng Li
Zhe Xu
Daqian Gao
Martin J. Falk
Stefano Sacanna
William T. M. Irvine
item.description:
Authors: Matteo Sabato, Sarah Chong, Yaocheng Li, Zhe Xu, Daqian Gao, Martin J. Falk, Stefano Sacanna, William T. M. Irvine
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 884-889
Abstract: Turbulence is chaotic, yet its fluctuations follow a structured, nonequilibrium energy cascade unconstrained by the equilibrium theorems that limit passive energy extraction from molecular gases. Here, we introduce turbulence shelters: hollow shells with a single aperture that filter eddies by scale, sustaining gradients in fluctuation intensity that drive directional particle transport despite zero mean fluid flux. Across three orders of magnitude in size, shelters establish particle concentration contrasts between their interior and the surrounding flow, with selectivity controlled by particle geometry, inertia, thermal fluctuations, and electrostatic forces. At the microscale, shelters discriminate particles differing by tens of nanometers independently of material composition. These results establish a design principle for selective filtration: Geometry that compartmentalizes turbulent fluctuations can harness ambient eddies to direct particle transport.

item.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area
item.dc:creator: Alexander B. Silva
Matthew K. Leonard
Patrick W. Hullett
Deborah F. Levy
Catherine Wang

Ilina Bhaya-Grossman
Edward F. Chang
item.description:
Authors: Alexander B. Silva, Matthew K. Leonard, Patrick W. Hullett, Deborah F. Levy, Catherine Wang, Duo Xu, Ilina Bhaya-Grossman, Edward F. Chang
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Article number: eaef8963
Abstract: Wernicke’s area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke’s area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke’s area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.

item.title: Meso–microporous zeolitic materials with thin walls containing ordered 10-ring channels
item.dc:creator: Zhenghan Zhang
Jiazheng Sun
Chao Ma
Xudong Tian
Mao Luo
Qike Jiang
Lei Han
Cong Lin
item.description:
Authors: Zhenghan Zhang, Jiazheng Sun, Chao Ma, Xudong Tian, Mao Luo, Qike Jiang, Lei Han, Cong Lin, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 907-912
Abstract: Aluminosilicate zeolites offer exceptional size and shape selectivity but suffer from diffusion limitations imposed by subnanometer micropores. Intrinsically meso–microporous zeolites integrate mesopores with micropores to create interconnected pathways that accelerate diffusion while preserving selectivity, yet their synthesis remains challenging. In this study, we report NJU120-5 and NJU120-7, intrinsically meso–microporous aluminosilicates that integrate micropores with mesopores enclosed by two-T-atom-thick walls containing 10-ring channels, forming a fully interconnected three-dimensional pore network. Their plausible framework models were established on the basis of advanced electron ptychographic imaging, revealing representative quasi-rectangular mesopores in calcined NJU120-5 with a uniform width of ~12 angstroms and lengths from 41 to 162 angstroms. Both materials exhibit high porosity, strong Brønsted acidity, and enhanced performance in heavy-oil cracking, delivering high yields of valuable fuels with suppressed coke formation.

item.title: The scientific record is never finished
item.dc:creator: Lauren Kmec
H. Holden Thorp
Valda Vinson
item.description:
Authors: Lauren Kmec, H. Holden Thorp, Valda Vinson
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 817-817
Abstract: The scholarly scientific record has always been a work in progress. From the earliest days of scientific publishing, new findings would come along that changed the way earlier findings are understood. When research journals were published only in print, occasional errors would be reported by the authors or found by others, and papers would be retracted or corrected. When publishing became digital, many more people could quickly access and scrutinize data and images for accuracy. Now, in the age of artificial intelligence (AI), it is possible for machines to do these examinations more expeditiously and at a larger scale. All of this has added an important new layer to the publishing process and put more responsibility on authors, who must update their work if new issues arise. In response to this need, Science is improving the ways in which it will flag and notate papers that require adjustment or where changes are under consideration. Our Editorial Policies now reflect these updates.

item.title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation
item.dc:creator: Xavier Rambout
Rina Nagao
Victor Gu
Sophie Werner
Justin Youngyunpipatkul
Jadon Schlierf
Christoph Pröschel
Lynne E. Maquat
item.description:
Authors: Xavier Rambout, Rina Nagao, Victor Gu, Sophie Werner, Justin Youngyunpipatkul, Jadon Schlierf, Christoph Pröschel, Lynne E. Maquat
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Article number: eaee8018
Abstract: Although RNA quality control tightly regulates gene expression, the scope of its regulatory functions in the nucleus remains unclear. In this study, we describe the quality control, on chromatin, of poised intron–containing polyadenylated RNAs (PIA-RNAs). Whether these precursor messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) constitute immature mRNAs whose splicing is pending or, alternatively, are degraded by the nuclear RNA exosome depends on whether they engage nuclear cap-binding protein 3 (NCBP3) or anillin, respectively. Many PIA-RNAs inversely controlled by NCBP3 and anillin encode mitochondrial factors. Thus, NCBP3 depletion in mouse as well as pathogenic mutations in the RNA exosome in humans result in reduced mitochondrial activity, muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination, and diminished motor coordination. Our findings reveal a competition between pre-mRNA metabolic pathways whose balance controls mitochondrial function and, when perturbed, leads to neurological diseases.

item.title: Balancing redox-mediated cytotoxicity and catalysis in natural product biosynthesis
item.dc:creator: Hannah A. Boesger
Emma Fang
Rongbin Wang
Ralph J. Harte

item.description:
Authors: Hannah A. Boesger, Emma Fang, Rongbin Wang, Ralph J. Harte, Arina Koroleva, Taylan Tunckanat, Areeba N. Momin, Sean J. Elliott, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 859-863
Abstract: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a conserved mechanism that coordinates three redox-mediated processes in secondary metabolite biosynthesis: self-protection, prevention of substrate degradation, and late-stage biosynthesis. Using the antitumor antibiotic doxorubicin as a model system, we show that the vicinal oxygen chelate (VOC) protein DnrV prevents reactive oxygen species formation and substrate degradation while promoting P450 catalysis. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. REACT represents a multifunctional protein class that balances antibiotic assembly, self-protection, and prevention of metabolite destruction, providing a foundational understanding of production of redox-active natural products.

item.dc:creator: Sukwoo Lee
Evan A. Weingarten

Authors: Sukwoo Lee, Evan A. Weingarten, Michael F. Reynolds, Kevin Sun, Alejandro J. Cortese, Huw M. L. Davies, Alyosha C. Molnar, Paul L. McEuen, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 875-883
Abstract: Real-time monitoring of chemical reactions is often achieved with specialized instrumentation along with custom-designed reactors or intrusive sampling. In this study, we introduce reaction telemetry, a wireless analytical strategy that enables remote, nonintrusive monitoring directly within operating reaction vessels. This approach uses light-powered microelectronic devices that communicate optically and function as autonomous sensing elements. We demonstrate continuous calorimetric measurements across diverse chemical reactions relevant to pharmaceutical and fine chemical synthesis, including photochemical and electrochemical systems, providing access to reaction kinetics under native operating conditions with subsecond temporal resolution. The resulting measurements will support catalyst evaluation, safety assessment, and mechanistic investigation and will accelerate data-driven reaction discovery. By embedding analytical functionality directly within reaction vessels, reaction telemetry establishes a general framework for information-rich observation of chemical processes across research, development, and education.

item.title: A DNA Typewriter records the cell lineage history of a mouse, from zygote to late organogenesis
item.dc:creator: Qi Yu
Haedong Kim
Sophie Seidel
James F. Acosta-Clark

Kyle O’Connor

item.description:
Authors: Qi Yu, Haedong Kim, Sophie Seidel, James F. Acosta-Clark, Beth K. Martin, Kyle O’Connor, Riza M. Daza, Molly Gasperini, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Article number: eael0508
Abstract: Mammalian biology unfolds over time, within tissues and organs opaque to our eyes and instruments. We applied DNA Typewriter, a sequential molecular recorder, to record the cell lineage of a mouse over nearly 2 weeks of development. From one embryo, we reconstructed a time-calibrated, parsimony-supported, zygote-rooted phylogeny of 1.28 million transcriptionally profiled cells. A burst of editing unequivocally marks the daughters of the first cleavage, which serve as inline replicates. We quantified clonal dominance arising during gastrulation. Tree siblings share cell type far above chance; heterotypic siblings mark terminal differentiations. Temporal sweeps of clade co-occurrence recover a dated hierarchy of cell type couplings; imputed labels for internal nodes recapitulate known state paths. A lineage-anchored ontogeny of mammalian development, long out of reach, is coming into view.

item.title: Interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer for low-loss soft ultrasonic interfaces
item.dc:creator: Shu Wang

item.description:
Authors: Shu Wang, Runze Li, Zihan Tang, Ying Li, Chen Gong, Won Jun Song, Chwee Teck Lim, Xiaodong Chen, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 895-900
Abstract: Ultrasound imaging relies on soft interfaces that transmit sound efficiently between a device and the body. Conventional gel couplants provide low acoustic loss but contain mobile liquid phases that can dry, flow, or leach during extended use. By contrast, mobile phase–free elastomers are more stable but generally attenuate megahertz ultrasound strongly, limiting their use as couplants. We report an interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer molecularly designed to overcome this trade-off. A densely grafted backbone lowers the shear modulus without increasing shear loss, whereas well-packed sidechains reduce bulk compressibility, jointly suppressing acoustic attenuation in a soft elastomer. The resulting elastomer combines soft tissue–like mechanics with low-loss acoustics, providing a durable couplant for soft ultrasonic interfaces.

Authors: Gina El Nesr, Simon L. Dürr, Irimpan I. Mathews, Qi Wen, Kewei Zhao, Ritimukta Sarangi, Ursula Rothlisberger, Fanny Sunden, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej3009
Abstract: De novo design of enzymes is a frontier challenge, requiring consideration of catalytic mechanism and optimization across biochemical and biophysical criteria. Here, we present dEVA (design by EVolutionary Algorithm), a multi-objective protein design method built on principles drawn from evolutionary biology. We apply dEVA to the zero-shot, de novo design of metalloenzymes by optimizing the coordination sphere of catalytic metals. We characterize a bi-zinc metalloenzyme that exhibits promiscuous hydrolytic activity towards both phosphomonoesters and phosphodiesters. This design achieves a rate enhancement ((k cat /K M )/k w ) of up to 3 x 10 13 relative to the uncatalyzed reaction, comparable to characterized natural phosphatases. Structural characterization via x-ray crystallography and absorption spectroscopy supports the design of a de novo active site. These results demonstrate that de novo enzymes can be designed without pre-specified motifs, natural templates, or evolutionary information.

item.dc:creator: Anna Maria Borruto
Tabea Kohlund
Lukas Rettig

item.description:
Authors: Anna Maria Borruto, Tabea Kohlund, Lukas Rettig, Martin von Renesse, Christian Alexander Hammer, Nikolas Leonhardt, Barbara Kurpiers, Claudia Calpe-López, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Pages: 864-869
Abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to–central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

item.dc:creator: Xu-Dong Hu
Yu-Qing Zheng

Tang-Yuan Li

item.description:
Authors: Xu-Dong Hu, Yu-Qing Zheng, Ke Zhai, Tang-Yuan Li, Zhi-Xin Guo, Jian-Ling Li, Wen-Bo Liu
Journal: Science; Article number: eaei2041
Abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge. Carbocation cascade cyclization is a textbook reaction that has transformed the synthesis of fused polycycles, but extending this strategy to bridged architectures requires precise control over highly reactive carbocation intermediates while overcoming the intrinsic energetic barrier of transannular cyclization. Herein, we report a quaternary-carbon-guided carbocation cascade rearrangement platform that enables enantioselective and divergent assembly of complex polycyclic architectures from readily available substrates. An enantioenriched quaternary center, installed via transition-metal-catalyzed allylation, serves as a temporary structural linchpin in an acid-triggered cationic cascade rearrangement process, forming multiple bonds and chiral centers in a single step. In combination with pre-embedded quaternary centers, this strategy provides bicyclic and bridged polycyclic frameworks bearing multiple stereocenters with high enantioselectivity.

item.title: Elastic-field reorganization stabilizes soft-lattice perovskites for durable solar cells
item.dc:creator: Biao Li
Tianchi Zhang

Yehui Wen

Xuegong Yu
Deren Yang
item.description:
Authors: Biao Li, Tianchi Zhang, Xingtao Wang, Yehui Wen, Yong Wang, Xuegong Yu, Deren Yang
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6826; Article number: eaeh3114
Abstract: The soft lattice that enables the exceptional performance of halide perovskites inherently compromises their operational stability. Here, we show that soft-lattice perovskites can be stabilized through elastic-field reorganization induced by rigid nanodiamond inclusions. Their inclusion enabled efficient bulk-to-boundary load transfer, redistributing and dissipating internal elastic fields at grain boundaries rather than allowing their accumulation within the crystal interior. Suppression of intergranular sliding constrained lattice deformation and mitigated defect generation during prolonged operation. Devices based on the stabilized perovskites with an area of 0.09 square centimeters achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.6%, and minimodules with an area of 16.1 square centimeters achieved 24.3%. These devices retained 80% of their initial PCE after 5000 hours of maximum power point operation at 85°C and 98% after 5000 hours of dynamically varying light-intensity day-night cycling.

Abstract: Reliable, strong, and low-loss interfaces are needed for durable perovskite photovoltaics. We have developed a molecular interface layer with an aromatic dual-site-binding ligand to improve the reliability of perovskite modules. The buried interface was strengthened through intermolecular interactions between the ligand and hole-selective layer and through strong chemical bonds. The resulting heterointerface enhances perovskite adhesion and releases interface strain, making the device more resilient to thermomechanical stresses. This device architecture achieves a power conversion efficiency of 22.7% for 900–square centimeter (cm 2 ) submodules (aperture area: 655 cm 2 ) and 21.3% for 7200-cm 2 standard modules (aperture area: 6380 cm 2 ). The champion 7200-cm 2 standard module maintained consistent performance during 105 days of outdoor testing, as independently measured by the Photovoltaic Accelerator for Commercializing Technologies (PACT) center.

item.title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
item.dc:creator: Xin Li
Guodong Ren
Haidong Lu
Kartik Samanta
Amit Kumar Shah
Kai Huang
Pravan Omprakash
Yu Yun
item.description:
Authors: Xin Li, Guodong Ren, Haidong Lu, Kartik Samanta, Amit Kumar Shah, Kai Huang, Pravan Omprakash, Yu Yun, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 763-767
Abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

item.title: Tracking danger on the peaks
item.dc:creator: Miriam Jackson
Amrit Thapa
item.description:
Authors: Miriam Jackson, Amrit Thapa
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 701-701
Abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

item.title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
item.dc:creator: Rebecca G. Englert
Matthieu J. B. Cartigny
Megan L. Baker
Sanem Acikalin
Dick Mastbergen
Niall Tracey
Sean C. Ruffell
Daniel H. Shugar
item.description:
Authors: Rebecca G. Englert, Matthieu J. B. Cartigny, Megan L. Baker, Sanem Acikalin, Dick Mastbergen, Niall Tracey, Sean C. Ruffell, Daniel H. Shugar, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 758-762
Abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

item.title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
item.dc:creator: Xuetao Ma
Zhaoyu Liu
Jiaqi Cai
Kenji Watanabe
Takashi Taniguchi
Xiaodong Xu
Jiun-Haw Chu
Matthew Yankowitz
item.description:
Authors: Xuetao Ma, Zhaoyu Liu, Jiaqi Cai, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xiaodong Xu, Jiun-Haw Chu, Matthew Yankowitz
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 768-772
Abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

item.description:
Authors: Siyuan He, Aatish Thennavan, Runmin Wei, Shanshan Bai, Jianzhuo Li, Chante Bethell, Emi Sei, Mitchell Rao, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaef4622
Abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

item.title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
item.dc:creator: Bo Su
Johan Rockström
Deliang Chen
Ingo Fetzer
Haipeng Feng
Gustaf Hugelius
Ricarda Winkelmann
Albert V. Norström
item.description:
Authors: Bo Su, Johan Rockström, Deliang Chen, Ingo Fetzer, Haipeng Feng, Gustaf Hugelius, Ricarda Winkelmann, Albert V. Norström, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaef5636
Abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

item.dc:creator: Yu Zhang

item.description:
Authors: Yu Zhang, Hu Nie, Zixuan Dai, Liying Zhao, Yihong Wan, Yi Wang, Yikang Chen, Xinhua Chen, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eady7788
Abstract: Strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy have largely focused on the intratumor immunosuppressive microenvironment, whereas approaches to amplify peripheral T cells and promote tumor recruitment have not been thoroughly explored. Using imaging mass cytometry in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), we observed T helper 1 (T H 1)–like immune architectures in mismatch repair–deficient tumors associated with response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immunotherapy. By contrast, mismatch repair–proficient (pMMR) tumors showed regulatory T–dominant spatial interactions. Clonal analyses revealed that stem-like CD4 + T cells differentiated into T H 1-like cells after PD-1 blockade. In pMMR CRC mouse models, combined OX40 agonist and PD-1 blockade suppressed tumor progression by expanding Il7r + early effector CD4 + intermediates in tumor-draining lymph nodes, promoting migration and connection with T H 1-like cells. This was accompanied by interferon-γ–dependent induction of immunostimulatory monocyte-macrophages and CD8 + effector T cells. These findings suggest that leveraging peripheral CD4 + T cell amplification may improve immunotherapy responses.

item.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
item.dc:creator: Carla M. Bellomo

item.description:
Authors: Carla M. Bellomo, Sebastian D. Kehl, Daniel O. Alonso, Natalia Periolo, Andrea Gaweda, Santiago Vidal-Freire, Hade Ramos, Martín Lammel, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej1679
Abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

item.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
item.dc:creator: J. A. Smiley-Rhodes
M. C. Bitter
S. Berardi
J. Beltz
D. A. Petrov
P. Schmidt
item.description:
Authors: J. A. Smiley-Rhodes, M. C. Bitter, S. Berardi, J. Beltz, D. A. Petrov, P. Schmidt
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaee0342
Abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

item.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
item.dc:creator: Anastasia E. Madsen
T. V. Pushpakumara
U. Sameera Weerathunga
Devaka K. Weerakoon
Shermin de Silva
item.description:
Authors: Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon, Shermin de Silva
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 792-798
Abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

C. H. Chen

item.description:
Authors: S. K. Betti, C. H. Chen, C. Xie, K. Worthen, S. Brittain, J. Najita, I. Rebollido, T. Beck, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 742-745
Abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

item.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
item.dc:creator: Bas B. Oude Munnink
Samuel Cordey

item.description:
Authors: Bas B. Oude Munnink, Samuel Cordey, Moussa Moïse Diagne, Jonathan Featherstone, Anabel Negredo, Sarah Temmam, Jenniffer Angulo, Carla M. Bellomo, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej1376
Abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
